title: Development delivery and quality
summary: Deliver working software that others can test and maintain.
why: Early workflow and integration checks reduce failures after launch.
Reproducible builds and handoffs let someone besides the original developer maintain the product.
know: Acceptance covers main paths, errors, permissions, compatibility, SEO and performance.
Use real-user data for Core Web Vitals. Lab scores help diagnose issues but do not establish field performance.
Separate development, staging and production. Keep secrets out of frontend code, repositories and test records.
inputs: Approved requirements, prototypes, content, supported devices and browsers
Repository, API contracts, test environment and acceptance criteria
actions: Read project rules and inspect the current implementation. Make the smallest suitable change.
Run checks appropriate to the risk. Verify data, permissions and main user paths.
Check mobile, keyboard use, performance and indexing; fix related failures.
Deliver a buildable version, running instructions, test evidence and known limits.
done: A clean environment can build the project; main paths have observed results.
Changes are reviewable and recoverable. List checks that were not run.
pitfalls: Treating a passing build as functional verification.
Mocking every dependency and claiming the integration works.
decision: Agree on acceptance and remaining risks. Fix issues that block main tasks.

reader.concept: Development is complete when users can finish their main tasks, understand failures and get help, and another maintainer can take over.
reader.when: Use this for website acceptance, code handoff or recurring defects.

example.situation: The homepage works, but a failed payment produces no message.
example.lesson: Test failure paths as well as normal screens.

reader.first_step: List the three most important tasks and how each can fail.
